set1.q: What does it usually mean when a patient develops symptoms from left bundle branch block?
opts: Severe heart disease
Correct. Most patients are asymptomatic; those who develop symptoms usually have severe underlying cardiac disease and so do not tolerate the block well.
A drug side effect only
Symptoms are not explained as a drug effect. They usually mean severe underlying cardiac disease that cannot tolerate the block.
A benign normal variant
A new right bundle branch block can occur without heart disease, but symptomatic left bundle branch block points to severe underlying heart disease.
An accessory pathway
An accessory pathway is the substrate of pre-excitation. Symptoms from left bundle branch block point to severe underlying cardiac disease.

set1.q: What does an implantable cardioverter defibrillator do?
opts: Detects fatal rhythms and shocks
Correct. The implantable cardioverter defibrillator prevents sudden cardiac death: sensing electrodes detect fatal arrhythmias and the device delivers a shock.
Paces only during bradycardia
Pacing a slow heart is the job of a pacemaker. A defibrillator detects fatal arrhythmias and shocks them, although newer ones can also pace.
Records the rhythm only
A recording-only device is a monitor. The implantable defibrillator detects fatal arrhythmias and delivers a shock.
Ablates an accessory pathway
Ablation is a catheter procedure, not a device function. The implantable defibrillator detects fatal arrhythmias and shocks them.

set1.q: Which are the main causes of frequent premature ventricular contractions?
opts: Hypertension and diabetes
Hypertension and diabetes drive degenerative conduction disease. Premature ventricular contractions come mainly from hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance.
Dehydration and fever
Dehydration and fever are not the named causes. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances head the list for premature ventricular contractions.
Hypoxemia, electrolytes

Correct. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalances (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia) are the main causes, so new frequent premature ventricular contractions call for checking oxygen and electrolytes.
Hyperthyroidism and anemia
Hyperthyroidism and anemia are causes of sinus tachycardia. Premature ventricular contractions are driven mainly by hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance.

set1.q: Once stabilized after unstable ventricular tachycardia, what do most patients need?
opts: Lifelong oral magnesium
Magnesium treats torsades acutely. Most survivors of unstable ventricular tachycardia need an implantable defibrillator.
No further treatment
Survivors remain at risk of sudden death; most need an implantable defibrillator for secondary prevention.
An implantable defibrillator
Correct. Once stabilized, most patients need an implantable cardioverter defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death from ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation.
A permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow conduction. Survivors of unstable ventricular tachycardia need a defibrillator for secondary prevention.

set1.q: Which is the first treatment for torsades de pointes in a conscious patient?
opts: Intravenous metoprolol
Beta blockers are avoided in torsades because the slower rate lengthens the QT. Magnesium is given first.
Intravenous magnesium
Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades, followed by more magnesium as an infusion.
Intravenous amiodarone
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.
Intravenous procainamide
Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium is the first treatment.

set1.q: Compared with Mobitz type I, Mobitz type II block carries a higher risk of which outcome?
opts: Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is not the feared progression. Mobitz type II tends to progress to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death.
Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia is not a complication of Mobitz type II. The danger is progression to complete heart block with a weak escape rhythm.
Mobitz type I block
Mobitz type II does not regress into the more benign Mobitz type I. Its risk is progression to complete heart block and sudden death.
Complete heart block
Correct. Mobitz type II has a higher risk of progression to complete (third-degree) heart block and sudden cardiac death, which is why it is treated even without symptoms.

set1.q: Which physiologic state is a named cause of Mobitz type I block?
opts: Increased vagal tone
Correct. Increased vagal tone from an overreactive vagus nerve is listed first among the causes of Mobitz type I, with nodal blocking drugs, Lyme carditis, ischemia and ablation.
High sympathetic tone
Sympathetic stimulation speeds atrioventricular conduction rather than blocking it. Increased vagal tone is the physiologic cause named for Mobitz type I.
Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism speeds the heart and is not a named cause of Mobitz type I. Increased vagal tone is the physiologic state listed.
Mild dehydration
Dehydration is not a named cause of Mobitz type I. The physiologic cause listed is increased vagal tone from an overreactive vagus nerve.

set1.q: After transcutaneous pacing stabilizes a patient in third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block, which is the definitive treatment?
opts: Wearable defibrillator
A wearable cardioverter defibrillator shocks lethal ventricular rhythms; it does not pace a slow escape rhythm. A permanent pacemaker is definitive.
Permanent pacemaker
Correct. Emergent transcutaneous pacing bridges the patient, and the definitive treatment for complete heart block is a permanent pacemaker.
Oral beta blocker
A beta blocker slows atrioventricular conduction and is itself a cause of block. Complete block is treated definitively with a permanent pacemaker.
Catheter ablation
Ablation destroys conduction tissue and is itself a named cause of complete block. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

set1.q: How is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia treated, even when the patient has a pulse?
opts: Defibrillation
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, only a short-lived transitional state, so it is defibrillated even if the patient looks well.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized shocks need a consistent QRS to time against. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated, even with a pulse.
Intravenous lidocaine alone
Drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never stable and is defibrillated.
Observation on a monitor
Watching is unsafe: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is a transitional state that needs defibrillation.

set1.q: What does the prognosis of left bundle branch block depend on?
opts: The patient's atrial rate
The atrial rate does not determine the outlook. The type and severity of underlying heart disease, and other conduction disturbances, do.
Serum magnesium level
Magnesium matters for torsades, not for the prognosis of bundle branch block, which depends on the underlying heart disease.
The underlying heart disease
Correct. Prognosis depends on the type and severity of the underlying heart disease and on whether other conduction disturbances are present.
The height of the R wave
R wave amplitude is not the determinant. Prognosis in left bundle branch block depends on the underlying heart disease and other conduction problems.

set1.q: For an elderly patient with Mobitz type II block found incidentally and causing no symptoms, which plan is appropriate?
opts: Permanent pacemaker
Correct. Mobitz type II is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression to complete block, and the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Reassurance only
Reassurance fits asymptomatic first-degree or Mobitz type I block. Mobitz type II needs a permanent pacemaker even without symptoms.
Recheck in a year
Waiting a year ignores the unpredictable progression of Mobitz type II to complete block and sudden death. A permanent pacemaker is the plan.
Start a beta blocker
A beta blocker slows atrioventricular conduction and is itself a cause of block. Mobitz type II is treated with a permanent pacemaker.

set1.q: Which PR interval pattern identifies Mobitz type I block?
opts: Fixed PR with random dropped QRS
A constant PR interval with random missing QRS complexes is Mobitz type II block, which arises lower in the His-Purkinje system and is more dangerous.
Fixed PR longer than 0.20 seconds
A constant PR interval over 0.20 seconds with every beat conducted is first-degree block. Mobitz type I lengthens the PR until a beat drops.
P waves unrelated to the QRS
Complete dissociation of P waves from QRS complexes is third-degree block. In Mobitz type I the P waves conduct with a lengthening delay.
PR lengthens until a QRS drops
Correct. In Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block the PR interval progressively increases from normal to long until a QRS complex is dropped, then the cycle repeats.

set1.q: For premature ventricular contractions under 1% of beats with no structural heart disease and no symptoms, which is the plan?
opts: Reassure and remove triggers
Correct. Low-risk patients with a low burden (under 1% or 1,000 a day), no structural heart disease and no symptoms need reassurance and elimination of triggers.
Lifelong beta blocker
A beta blocker is first-line only when low-risk patients have symptoms. Silent, low-burden beats need reassurance and removal of triggers.
Catheter ablation
Ablation is kept for refractory symptoms or cardiomyopathy. Low-burden, silent beats in a normal heart need only reassurance.
Implantable defibrillator
An implantable defibrillator is for prevention of sudden death from lethal rhythms, not for occasional benign ectopic beats.

set1.q: What decides how severe the symptoms of third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block are?
opts: Serum potassium alone
Potassium is not the stated determinant. Severity depends on the escape rate, the site of the escape rhythm and underlying heart disease.
The patient's age alone
Age is not the stated determinant. Symptoms depend on the ventricular escape rate, where the escape rhythm arises and underlying heart disease.
Escape rate, site, heart disease
Correct. Symptoms range from none to severe and depend on the ventricular escape rate, the site of the escape rhythm and the presence of underlying heart disease.
Atrial rate and P wave shape
The atrial rate and P wave shape do not decide symptoms, because the P waves are not conducted. The ventricular escape rate and its site do.

set1.q: Which two arrest rhythms are shockable?
opts: Tachycardia, pulseless electrical
Pulseless electrical activity is unshockable. The shockable pair is ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia.
Fibrillation, pulseless tachycardia
Correct. Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are treated with defibrillation; asystole and pulseless electrical activity are unshockable.
Asystole and fibrillation
Asystole has no electrical activity to reset and is unshockable. Fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are the shockable pair.
Pulseless electrical, asystole
Pulseless electrical activity and asystole are both unshockable and are treated with compressions and epinephrine.

set1.q: Sudden cardiac death is defined as unexpected natural death from cardiac causes within what time of collapse?
opts: Thirty days
Thirty days is an outcome window, not the definition. Sudden cardiac death occurs within 1 hour of collapse.
One hour
Correct. Sudden cardiac death is generally defined as unexpected natural death from cardiac causes occurring within 1 hour of the patient's collapse.
Ten minutes
Ten minutes is too short a window. The definition counts unexpected cardiac death within 1 hour of collapse.
Six hours
Six hours is not the window used. Sudden cardiac death is death within 1 hour of collapse.

set1.q: Which is the management of asymptomatic first-degree atrioventricular block?
opts: Intravenous amiodarone
Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation; it has no role in first-degree block, which needs no treatment when silent.
No treatment needed
Correct. No treatment is needed unless the patient has debilitating symptoms or heart failure symptoms; the vast majority of first-degree blocks cause none.
Permanent pacemaker
A permanent pacemaker is considered only for symptomatic first-degree block. An asymptomatic patient needs no treatment.
Transcutaneous pacing
Transcutaneous pacing is an emergency bridge for unstable high-grade block such as Mobitz type II or complete block, not for a stable, silent first-degree block.

set1.q: Which history places a patient with premature ventricular contractions in the high-risk group?
opts: Daily caffeine use
Caffeine is a trigger to remove, not a high-risk feature. A history of syncope places the patient in the high-risk group.
Age under 30
Young age is not a high-risk feature. Prior syncope, a high burden, cardiomyopathy or structural disease define high risk.
Occasional anxiety
Anxiety is not on the high-risk list. A history of syncope is one of the features that make a patient high risk.
Prior syncope
Correct. High-risk features are a burden over 15%, premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy, pre-existing structural or conduction disease and a history of syncope.

set1.q: Which acute event can cause right bundle branch block by suddenly raising right ventricular pressure?
opts: Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection loads the left side and the aorta, not the right ventricle. Pulmonary embolism is the acute cause named.
Hypertensive crisis
A hypertensive crisis raises left ventricular afterload. The acute right ventricular pressure load named is pulmonary embolism.
Acute gastroenteritis
Gastroenteritis does not load the right ventricle. A pulmonary embolism suddenly raises right ventricular pressure and can cause the block.
Pulmonary embolism
Correct. A sudden increase in right ventricular pressure, as from a pulmonary embolism, is a named cause of right bundle branch block.

set1.q: Which arrest rhythms carry the best prognosis?
opts: Asystole only
Asystole carries a poor prognosis. Ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation have the best prognosis of the arrest rhythms.
Ventricular tachycardia, fibrillation
Correct. Among cardiac arrest rhythms, ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation have the best prognosis; asystole and pulseless electrical activity are poor.
Asystole, pulseless electrical
Asystole and pulseless electrical activity have a poor prognosis and are usually end-of-life rhythms.
Pulseless electrical activity only
Pulseless electrical activity has a poor prognosis. Ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation carry the best prognosis.

set1.q: Which parasitic infection is a named cause of third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block?
opts: Giardiasis
Giardiasis is an intestinal infection that does not reach the conduction system. Chagas disease is the parasitic cause named for complete block.
Chagas disease
Correct. Chagas disease is listed among the causes of complete block, with Lyme carditis, bacterial endocarditis with an abscess and inflammatory or infiltrative disease.
Malaria
Malaria is not a named cause of complete block. The parasitic infection listed is Chagas disease.
Toxoplasmosis
Toxoplasmosis is not on the list of causes of complete block. Chagas disease is the parasitic cause named.

set1.q: Which drug is given repeatedly during cardiac arrest from ventricular fibrillation, alongside shocks and cardiopulmonary resuscitation?
opts: Adenosine
Adenosine is for narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia. Epinephrine is the repeated drug in cardiac arrest.
Epinephrine
Correct. Epinephrine is given by intravenous or intraosseous push at intervals throughout the arrest, alongside defibrillation and high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
Norepinephrine
Norepinephrine is an infusion for shock with a pulse, not the arrest drug. Epinephrine is given repeatedly during cardiac arrest.
Dopamine
Dopamine is not part of the arrest steps. Epinephrine is the drug given repeatedly during cardiac arrest.

set1.q: For hemodynamically stable, sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, which approach is used?
opts: Intravenous antiarrhythmic

Correct. Stable, monomorphic sustained ventricular tachycardia is pharmacologically cardioverted with intravenous lidocaine, amiodarone or procainamide, after a monitor, intravenous access, a 12-lead electrocardiogram, oxygen and labs.
Immediate defibrillation
Defibrillation is for pulseless or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. A stable monomorphic rhythm with a pulse gets an intravenous antiarrhythmic.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is for the unstable patient who still has a pulse. A stable patient is cardioverted with drugs first.
Intravenous adenosine
Adenosine targets atrioventricular nodal rhythms. Stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is treated with an intravenous antiarrhythmic.

set1.q: In an elderly patient, which named cause of right bundle branch block reflects aging of the conduction system?
opts: Sudden pulmonary embolism
A pulmonary embolism is an acute cause at any age through a sudden rise in right ventricular pressure, not a reflection of aging.
Viral myocarditis
Myocarditis is an inflammatory cause at any age. The aging-related cause listed first is degenerative change of the conduction system.
Accessory pathway
An accessory pathway causes pre-excitation and is not a cause of right bundle branch block. Age-related degeneration is.
Age-related degeneration
Correct. Age-related degenerative change of the conduction system heads the list of causes of right bundle branch block, as it does for first-degree block.

set1.q: Unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse is treated with what?
opts: Intravenous amiodarone
An intravenous antiarrhythmic is for the stable patient. Instability with a pulse calls for synchronized cardioversion.
Transcutaneous pacing
Pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms. Unstable ventricular tachycardia with a pulse is treated with synchronized cardioversion.
Synchronized cardioversion
Correct. In unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, check for a pulse: with a pulse, synchronized cardioversion; without one, defibrillation.
Defibrillation
Defibrillation (unsynchronized) is for the pulseless patient. With a pulse, unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia gets synchronized cardioversion.

set1.q: Which chronic pulmonary vascular condition is a named cause of right bundle branch block?
opts: Pleural effusion
A pleural effusion is fluid around the lung, not a pulmonary vascular disease. Pulmonary hypertension is the named chronic cause.
Obstructive sleep apnea
Sleep apnea is not on the list of causes. Pulmonary hypertension, which strains the right ventricle, is named.
Chronic sinusitis
Sinusitis is an upper airway condition and not a named cause. Pulmonary hypertension is the chronic cause listed.
Pulmonary hypertension
Correct. Pulmonary hypertension is a named cause of right bundle branch block, along with age-related degeneration, ischemic heart disease, cardiomyopathies and inflammatory or infiltrative disease.

set1.q: Which treatment is used for symptomatic left bundle branch block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
opts: Intravenous magnesium
Magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes. Symptomatic left bundle branch block with reduced ejection fraction gets a biventricular pacer.
Catheter ablation
Ablation destroys tissue and would not restore left ventricular activation. The named treatment is a biventricular pacemaker.
Biventricular pacemaker
Correct. Left bundle branch block is usually left untreated, except symptomatic block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which is treated with a biventricular pacer.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion terminates tachycardias with a pulse. It cannot correct a conduction delay; a biventricular pacer resynchronizes the ventricles.

set1.q: What are the two leading causes of pulseless electrical activity in adults?
opts: Hyperkalemia and acidosis
Potassium disturbances and acidosis are reversible causes of arrest, but the two leading causes of pulseless electrical activity are hypovolemia and hypoxia.
Tamponade and pneumothorax
Tamponade and tension pneumothorax are reversible causes, yet the two leading causes named are hypovolemia and hypoxia.
Hypothermia and toxins
Hypothermia and toxins are reversible causes of arrest, but hypovolemia and hypoxia lead for pulseless electrical activity.
Hypovolemia and hypoxia

Adenosine

Digoxin has no role in cardiac arrest. Amiodarone is the antiarrhythmic for fibrillation that persists after shocks.

Act as pacemakers
Correct. Newer implantable defibrillators can also act as pacemakers, in addition to sensing fatal arrhythmias and delivering a shock.

Patients with Lyme disease

Symptomatic patients
Correct. A permanent pacemaker is considered for patients whose first-degree block causes symptoms, typically once the PR interval exceeds 0.3 seconds; otherwise no treatment is needed.

Age alone is not an indication. Most older adults with first-degree block are asymptomatic and need no treatment; pacing is for symptoms.

set2.q: Which finding defines third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block?
opts: Prolonged but constant PR interval
A prolonged constant PR with every beat conducted is first-degree block. Complete block has no consistent PR because nothing conducts.
P waves and QRS complexes unrelated
Correct. In complete block no P waves are conducted, so the atria and ventricles are completely dissociated and beat at two different regular rates.

A PR that lengthens before a dropped beat is Mobitz type I block, where P waves still conduct, just with a growing delay.
Constant PR with random dropped QRS
A constant PR with occasional dropped QRS complexes is Mobitz type II. In complete block no P wave conducts at all.

set2.q: Why is Mobitz type II block treated as dangerous even without symptoms?
opts: Leads to atrial fibrillation

Signals digoxin toxicity
Mobitz type II comes mostly from His-Purkinje disease, not digoxin. It is dangerous because of unpredictable progression to complete block.
Unpredictable progression
Correct. Guidelines treat Mobitz type II as dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression to complete heart block and its poor prognosis.
Frequent heart failure
Heart failure is not the stated reason. Mobitz type II is dangerous because it can progress unpredictably to complete block and sudden death.

set2.q: When right bundle branch block causes symptoms, what do they usually point to?
opts: Severe underlying heart disease
Correct. Right bundle branch block is usually asymptomatic; patients who develop symptoms usually have severe underlying cardiac disease, with heart failure-like symptoms.
A harmless normal variant
A new right bundle branch block can be benign when silent, but symptoms usually point to severe underlying heart disease.
An accessory pathway
An accessory pathway causes pre-excitation, not bundle branch block symptoms. Symptoms usually point to severe underlying heart disease.
Isolated electrolyte loss
Electrolyte disturbances drive premature ventricular contractions. Symptomatic right bundle branch block points to severe underlying heart disease.

set2.q: Which feature separates Mobitz type I from Mobitz type II block?
opts: Whether the QRS complexes are narrow
Both types are described with a narrow QRS, so QRS width does not separate them. The lengthening versus constant PR interval does.
Whether the atrial rate is regular
The P waves are uniform and regular in both types. What differs is whether the PR interval lengthens before the dropped beat.
Whether the PR lengthens before a drop
Correct. Mobitz type I shows a progressively lengthening PR interval before the dropped QRS; Mobitz type II keeps a constant PR and drops QRS complexes at random.
Whether any P waves fail to conduct
Both types of second-degree block have P waves that fail to conduct, so more P waves than QRS complexes. The PR behavior is what separates them.

set2.q: Which electrocardiogram findings define asystole?
opts: Wide beats at 30 a minute
Slow wide beats are an escape rhythm. Asystole has no rate, rhythm, P waves or QRS complexes.
No rate, rhythm, P or QRS
Correct. Asystole (ventricular standstill) has a rate of zero, no rhythm, no P waves, no PR interval and no QRS complexes.
Chaotic, uncoordinated waves
Chaotic, uncoordinated activity is ventricular fibrillation, which is shockable. Asystole has no activity at all.
Organized beats, no pulse
Organized beats without a pulse define pulseless electrical activity. Asystole shows no electrical activity.

set2.q: Besides old age, which chronic conditions drive the degenerative His-Purkinje disease behind Mobitz type II block?
opts: Asthma and eczema
Asthma and eczema are not named causes. The degenerative His-Purkinje disease behind Mobitz type II is linked to old age, hypertension and diabetes.
Gout and osteoarthritis
Gout and osteoarthritis are not named causes. Chronic hypertension and diabetes, with old age, drive the degenerative conduction disease.
Migraine and anxiety
Migraine and anxiety are not named causes. The degenerative His-Purkinje disease of Mobitz type II is tied to age, hypertension and diabetes.
Hypertension and diabetes
Correct. Degenerative His-Purkinje disease, the most common cause of Mobitz type II, comes especially from old age, chronic hypertension and diabetes.

set2.q: Which infiltrative diseases are named causes of third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block?
opts: Asthma and emphysema
Asthma and emphysema are lung diseases, not infiltrative heart disease. Amyloidosis and sarcoidosis are the named causes.
Amyloidosis and sarcoidosis
Correct. Inflammatory and infiltrative disease, namely myocarditis, amyloidosis and sarcoidosis, is listed among the causes of complete heart block.
Cirrhosis and pancreatitis
Cirrhosis and pancreatitis do not infiltrate the conduction system. Amyloidosis and sarcoidosis are the infiltrative causes named.
Osteoporosis and gout
Osteoporosis and gout are not named causes. The infiltrative diseases listed for complete block are amyloidosis and sarcoidosis.

set2.q: Which kind of shock is delivered for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a consistent QRS and suits unstable monomorphic rhythm with a pulse. Polymorphic rhythm is defibrillated.
A low-energy timed shock
A timed shock is synchronized cardioversion, which needs a consistent QRS. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia gets unsynchronized defibrillation.
No shock, only drugs
Drugs alone are for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never stable and is defibrillated.
Unsynchronized defibrillation
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable and its QRS shape keeps changing, so it is defibrillated (unsynchronized) even when a pulse is present.

opts: Gastritis and esophagitis

Sinusitis and bronchitis
Sinusitis and bronchitis are not named causes. The inflammatory causes of Mobitz type II are myocarditis and reactive arthritis.
Myocarditis, reactive arthritis
Correct. Inflammatory disease such as myocarditis and reactive arthritis is listed among the causes of Mobitz type II, with His-Purkinje degeneration, Lyme carditis, infarction and ablation.
Pericarditis and pleurisy
Pericarditis and pleurisy are not on the list. The inflammatory causes of Mobitz type II named are myocarditis and reactive arthritis.

set2.q: Which is the most common predisposing condition for sudden cardiac death?
opts: Coronary artery disease
Correct. Coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition for sudden cardiac death, even in patients without a history of myocardial infarction.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an important cause in young people, but coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition overall.
Long QT syndrome
Long QT syndrome predisposes to torsades de pointes, but coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition for sudden death.
An accessory pathway
An accessory pathway can allow dangerous pre-excited rhythms, yet coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition.

opts: Wearable defibrillator vest
Correct. There is a wearable (external) cardioverter defibrillator, worn as a vest, that detects fatal ventricular arrhythmias and delivers a shock.
Implantable loop recorder
A loop recorder is implanted and only records the rhythm. The wearable cardioverter defibrillator vest is the external device that shocks.
Ambulatory Holter monitor
A Holter monitor records the rhythm for a day or two but cannot shock. The wearable defibrillator vest detects and shocks fatal rhythms.
Transcutaneous pacing pads
Transcutaneous pacing pads pace a slow heart in an emergency. The wearable defibrillator vest is the worn device that shocks.

Correct. Procainamide is avoided when the QT is prolonged or the patient has congestive heart failure, because it lengthens the QT and depresses the heart.
Asthma or chronic bronchitis
Lung disease is not the named caution. Procainamide is avoided with a prolonged QT or congestive heart failure.
Hypothyroidism or anemia
These are not the named cautions. Procainamide is avoided with a prolonged QT or heart failure.
Diabetes or obesity
Neither is the stated caution. Procainamide should be avoided with a prolonged QT or congestive heart failure.

set2.q: Which is the most common cause of first-degree atrioventricular block?
opts: Atrioventricular node ischemia
Atrioventricular node ischemia, usually after a myocardial infarction, is a recognized cause, but the most common cause is age-related degenerative change.
Overactive vagal tone
Increased vagal tone from an overreactive vagus nerve can prolong the PR interval, yet age-related degeneration of the conduction system is the most common cause.
Age-related conduction degeneration
Correct. Age-related degenerative change of the conduction system is the most common cause: the pathway wears out, so the impulse takes longer to cross the atrioventricular node.
Lyme disease of the heart
Lyme disease is a named infectious cause of first-degree block, but it is far less common than age-related degeneration of the conduction system.

set2.q: In third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block, where can the non-conducted P waves be found?
opts: Nowhere: atria are silent
The atria are not silent in complete block; they keep firing at their own rate. The P waves are simply not conducted and may be buried in other waves.
Inverted after each QRS
Inverted P waves after the QRS describe retrograde junctional activity. In complete block the upright, uniform P waves march through at their own rate.
Buried in QRS, ST segment or T wave
Correct. The P waves keep their uniform shape and regular rate, with no association to the QRS complexes, so they may be buried in the QRS complex, ST segment or T wave.
Only before each QRS complex
A P wave before every QRS is the normal pattern of conducted beats. In complete block the P waves fall anywhere, even inside the QRS, ST segment or T wave.

opts: They interact with magnesium
No interaction with magnesium is the reason. Beta blockers slow the rate and so indirectly prolong the QT.
Bradycardia lengthens the QT
Correct. Beta blockers cause bradycardia and lengthen the R to R interval, which indirectly prolongs the QT and worsens acquired torsades.
They cause hypokalemia
Beta blockers are not avoided for causing hypokalemia. The concern is bradycardia, which indirectly lengthens the QT.
They shorten the QT too much
Beta blockers do not dangerously shorten the QT. By slowing the rate they indirectly prolong it.

opts: Defibrillation and amiodarone
Shocks and amiodarone are for shockable rhythms. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity rely on compressions and epinephrine.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable tachycardia with a pulse. Unshockable arrest rhythms get compressions and epinephrine.
Magnesium and lidocaine
Magnesium and lidocaine belong to torsades and shock-refractory fibrillation. Compressions and epinephrine are the mainstays here.
Compressions and epinephrine
Correct. High-quality chest compressions and epinephrine by intravenous or intraosseous push at intervals are the mainstays, with early intubation considered.

Anxiety symptoms are not described. Symptomatic left bundle branch block looks like a heart failure exacerbation with exertional dyspnea.
Hypoglycemia
Low blood glucose is not the comparison. Symptoms resemble a heart failure exacerbation: dizziness, shortness of breath and dyspnea on exertion.
Heart failure
Correct. Symptomatic left bundle branch block resembles a congestive heart failure exacerbation, with dizziness, shortness of breath and dyspnea on exertion.
Asthma attack
Wheezing bronchospasm is not the picture. Symptoms from left bundle branch block resemble a heart failure exacerbation.

opts: Magnesium
Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, and more magnesium is then given as an infusion; it is the main treatment.
Potassium
Low potassium is a cause of a long QT and should be corrected, but the drug that breaks torsades is intravenous magnesium.
Calcium
Low calcium is a cause of a long QT, yet calcium is not the treatment that breaks torsades. Magnesium is.
Phosphate
Phosphate plays no named role in torsades. Intravenous magnesium, then a magnesium infusion, is the treatment.

opts: Glomerulonephritis
Glomerulonephritis affects the kidneys, not the conduction system. The endocarditis complication tied to complete block is an abscess.
An associated abscess
Correct. Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is listed among the causes of complete block, because the infection can extend into the conduction system.
Splinter hemorrhages
Splinter hemorrhages are a peripheral sign of endocarditis in the nail beds and do not cause block. An abscess near the conduction system does.
Septic lung emboli
Septic emboli to the lungs do not interrupt cardiac conduction. Endocarditis causes complete block when an abscess forms.

opts: Over 1% of beats
One percent is the low-burden line: under 1% (or 1,000 a day) with no heart disease and no symptoms is low risk. High risk starts above 15%.
Over 0.5% of beats
A burden of 0.5% is low and calls for reassurance when the heart is normal. The high-risk burden is over 15% of beats.
Any single ectopic
A single ectopic beat is common and benign. The high-risk burden is over 15% of beats, or 15,000 a day.
Over 15% of beats

Correct. A high burden, over 15% of beats or 15,000 a day, is one of the high-risk features, with premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy, structural or conduction disease and syncope.

set2.q: Which electrocardiogram finding defines first-degree atrioventricular block?
opts: PR lengthening until a QRS drops
A PR interval that grows longer until a QRS complex is dropped is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block. In first-degree block every P wave conducts.
Constant PR with random dropped QRS
A constant PR interval with random missing QRS complexes is Mobitz type II block. First-degree block has a long PR but never drops a beat.
P waves unrelated to the QRS
P waves with no relationship to the QRS complexes describe complete (third-degree) block. In first-degree block each P wave is followed by a QRS.
Constant PR interval over 0.20 seconds
Correct. First-degree atrioventricular block is a prolonged PR interval, greater than 0.20 seconds and constant, with one P wave for every narrow QRS complex.

opts: Aortic stenosis
Correct. Valvular heart disease, especially aortic stenosis, is a named cause of left bundle branch block, along with chronic hypertension, ischemic heart disease and dilated cardiomyopathy.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium and is not singled out. Aortic stenosis is the valve lesion named for left bundle branch block.
Pulmonic stenosis
Pulmonic stenosis loads the right ventricle and is not the lesion named. Aortic stenosis is singled out for left bundle branch block.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation is a right-sided lesion. The valve disease singled out for left bundle branch block is aortic stenosis.

set2.q: Because Mobitz type II block usually originates at the bundle of His, what is true of its escape rhythm?
opts: Fast and narrow
A fast, narrow escape rhythm would come from higher in the junction. A block at the bundle of His leaves a weak, unreliable escape rhythm.
Sinus driven
The sinoatrial node keeps firing, but its impulses are blocked below. The escape rhythm that takes over is weak and unreliable.
Always over 60
A low escape rhythm is slow, not above 60 per minute. With a block at the bundle of His the escape rhythm is weak and unreliable.
Weak and unreliable
Correct. Because the block sits low, at the bundle of His, the escape rhythm is weak and unreliable, which adds to the risk of sudden death.

set2.q: Which electrolyte disturbances are named triggers of premature ventricular contractions?
opts: High phosphate, low chloride
Phosphate and chloride are not named. The electrolyte triggers listed are hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia.
Low potassium, low magnesium
Correct. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, along with hypercalcemia, are the electrolyte imbalances named as causes of premature ventricular contractions.
High potassium, low sodium
Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia are not the named triggers. Low potassium, low magnesium and high calcium are listed.
Low calcium, high sodium

set2.q: Most torsades de pointes is due to which cause?
opts: Congenital long QT syndrome
Congenital long QT syndrome does cause torsades, but most cases are due to acquired long QT syndrome.
Acute myocardial ischemia
Acute ischemia is the most common cause of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia without a prolonged QT. Torsades is mostly acquired long QT.
Accessory pathway
An accessory pathway causes pre-excitation, not torsades. Most torsades is due to acquired long QT syndrome.
Acquired long QT syndrome
Correct. Most torsades de pointes is due to acquired long QT syndrome, from drugs or from hypokalemia and hypocalcemia, rather than the congenital syndrome.

set2.q: Which drugs are named for pharmacologic cardioversion of stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Metoprolol, verapamil, digoxin
Rate-slowing agents are not the named cardioversion drugs. Intravenous lidocaine, amiodarone or procainamide are.
Lidocaine, amiodarone, procainamide
Correct. If hemodynamically stable and monomorphic, sustained ventricular tachycardia is cardioverted pharmacologically with intravenous lidocaine, amiodarone or procainamide.
Adenosine, diltiazem, digoxin
These act on the atrioventricular node for supraventricular rhythms. The named drugs are intravenous lidocaine, amiodarone or procainamide.
Magnesium, calcium, potassium
Magnesium treats torsades; calcium and potassium are not named. Lidocaine, amiodarone or procainamide cardiovert stable monomorphic rhythm.

set2.q: What is the first treatment for ventricular fibrillation?
opts: Transcutaneous pacing
Pacing treats a slow, organized rhythm. Ventricular fibrillation is defibrillated as soon as possible.
Immediate defibrillation
Correct. Ventricular fibrillation is treated as cardiac arrest: start cardiopulmonary resuscitation, give oxygen, attach the monitor and defibrillate (unsynchronized) as soon as possible.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion needs a QRS to time against. Fibrillation has none and is defibrillated as soon as possible.
Intravenous amiodarone
Amiodarone is added for fibrillation that persists after shocks. The first treatment is defibrillation as soon as possible.

set2.q: Which mechanism makes atrioventricular block more common in elderly patients?
opts: Degenerative conduction disease
Correct. Age-related degenerative change of the conduction system is the most common cause of first-degree block and drives the His-Purkinje disease behind Mobitz type II and complete block.
Rising vagal tone with age
Increased vagal tone is a cause of first-degree and Mobitz type I block, but it is not the age-linked mechanism. Degeneration of the conduction system is.
Age-related Lyme exposure
Lyme carditis is an infectious cause at any age, not an age-related mechanism. Elderly patients develop block from degenerative conduction disease.
Shrinking atrial size
Atrial size is not the stated mechanism. Elderly patients develop block through degenerative change of the conduction system.

set2.q: Which is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II block?
opts: Permanent pacemaker
Correct. The definitive treatment for Mobitz type II block is a permanent pacemaker, because the block can progress unpredictably to complete heart block and sudden death.
Transcutaneous pacing
Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent, temporary measure that bridges the patient to definitive therapy, which is a permanent pacemaker.
Catheter ablation
Catheter ablation destroys tissue and is itself a named cause of Mobitz type II. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Implantable defibrillator
An implantable cardioverter defibrillator shocks lethal ventricular rhythms. A failing conduction system needs a permanent pacemaker instead.
